title: Juneteenth: History, Meaning and Cannabis Justice

body:
What is Juneteenth? It marks June 19, 1865, when a Union general in Galveston, Texas, announced that all enslaved people in the state were free. Today it's a federal holiday and a day for both celebration and reflection. Here's the Juneteenth history behind it, how it became a national holiday, and why unequal cannabis enforcement belongs in the conversation.

## What happened on June 19, 1865

President Abraham Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation on January 1, 1863. In Texas, freedom took far longer to arrive. On the morning of June 19, 1865, Union Major General Gordon Granger arrived in Galveston with General Order No. 3, informing the people of Texas that all enslaved people in the state were free.

That was two and a half years after the proclamation. According to the National Archives, the order delivered freedom to some 250,000 people who were still enslaved in Texas.

## How Juneteenth became a federal holiday

One year later, on June 19, 1866, freed people in Galveston organized the first annual celebration of emancipation in Texas. Early gatherings also served the community in practical ways, including sharing information about voting. In 1872, four Houston church leaders bought 10 acres in the city's Third Ward to be used only for emancipation celebrations.

The tradition faced headwinds. During the Great Migration, many Black Texans moved north and west, and distance from family and factory work made the old celebrations harder to keep. Interest returned in the 1950s and 1960s, as people tied the civil rights movement to the meaning of emancipation. By the early 1970s, Juneteenth celebrations were emerging in cities such as Chicago, Los Angeles, Oakland, Seattle and Minneapolis.

On June 17, 2021, President Joe Biden signed the Juneteenth National Independence Day Act, adding June 19 to the country's legal public holidays. As of 2026, all 50 states and the District of Columbia recognize the day as a holiday or observance.

## Why the day still invites reflection

Juneteenth celebrates freedom, and it also marks how long freedom was withheld from people who were already free on paper. That gap between what the law promised and what people lived through is part of why the day still resonates. It's a time to honor resilience, family and community, and to look honestly at where equality still falls short.

## The war on drugs and unequal cannabis enforcement

Cannabis enforcement is one place where that gap is easy to measure, and the war on drugs' racial impact shows up plainly in arrest data. An ACLU report published in 2020 examined marijuana arrests from 2010 to 2018. Police made more than 6.1 million marijuana-related arrests over that span. In 2018, Black people were arrested for possession at 3.64 times the per-capita rate of white people nationwide, up from 3.31 in 2010, even though the two groups use marijuana at similar rates.

An arrest or conviction can follow a person for years, affecting work, housing and more long after the case closes. Our history of the [war on drugs](/blog/war-on-drugs-cannabis-history/) traces how those policies took shape.

## Repair efforts: expungement, equity programs and reinvestment

- **Clearing records.** Presidential pardon proclamations in October 2022 and December 2023 covered certain federal offenses related to marijuana possession. A presidential pardon can't reach state convictions, so state records depend on state law. If you have an old Michigan marijuana record, our [Michigan expungement guide](/blog/michigan-marijuana-expungement/) is a good place to begin.
- **Equity programs.** Some states have created cannabis equity programs that offer licensing support to people and neighborhoods most affected by past enforcement. Our article on [cannabis social equity](/blog/cannabis-social-equity/) looks at how these programs work.
- **Reinvestment.** As of October 2026, Illinois's Restore, Reinvest, and Renew program directs 25% of the state's adult-use cannabis tax revenue to grants. They go to communities hit hardest by economic disinvestment, violence and the war on drugs.

## Ways to observe Juneteenth

- **Learn.** Read the history of General Order No. 3, visit a museum exhibit or attend a local history talk.
- **Support Black-owned businesses,** in cannabis and beyond, and listen to the people building them.
- **Volunteer or donate** with groups working on reentry, record clearing and fair policy. Our list of [cannabis advocacy organizations](/blog/cannabis-advocacy-organizations/) is a good starting point.
- **Gather and celebrate.** Juneteenth began as a community celebration, and sharing a meal, music and stories honors that history.

Juneteenth is one of several heritage observances on our blog, alongside [Black History Month](/blog/celebrating-black-history-month/) and [Hispanic Heritage Month](/blog/hispanic-heritage-month/).

faq.a: Juneteenth commemorates June 19, 1865, when Union Major General Gordon Granger arrived in Galveston, Texas, with General Order No. 3, announcing that all enslaved people in the state were free. It came two and a half years after the Emancipation Proclamation, and it brought freedom to some 250,000 people still enslaved in Texas.

faq.q: When did Juneteenth become a federal holiday?
faq.a: On June 17, 2021, President Joe Biden signed the Juneteenth National Independence Day Act, which added June 19 to the list of legal public holidays. Communities had celebrated the day long before that, starting in 1866, when freed people in Galveston held the first annual emancipation celebration in Texas.

faq.q: How did cannabis laws affect Black communities?
faq.a: Unequally. An ACLU report found that in 2018 a Black person’s risk of a marijuana possession arrest was 3.64 times a white person’s, despite similar rates of use. Those arrests could shape jobs and housing for years, which is why record clearing and equity programs matter.

review.notes: Overlap clean-up 2026-10-24: a local 8-word shingle check against every other blog article and site page (positive control fired) found two shared runs in this check's corrected 2018 takeaway; reworded, figure unchanged, re-check shows none. Independent fact-check 2026-10-24. National Archives exhibit and blog, the Handbook of Texas, the DOJ pardon and FAQ pages, the Illinois R3 page and the CRS fact sheet opened with WebFetch; Public Law 117-17 and the National Archives blog re-read with curl; the ACLU report PDF read with pdftotext. Two wrong claims: the ACLU 3.64 ratio is the 2018 figure (2010 was 3.31), not a 2010-2018 average, and state recognition is now all 50 states plus DC (CRS, June 2026). Sources grew from six to eight (DOJ FAQ, CRS); the article is low risk, so the six-source cap for medical and legal pieces does not apply. Writer's notes: Final read 2026-10-24 (batch 13 resume): all six sources re-opened. Fixed: the draft said celebrations spread to Chicago and other cities with the Great Migration; the National Archives says the migration made celebrations harder to keep and the big-city celebrations emerged in the early 1970s after a 1950s-60s revival. Houston land buyers corrected to four church leaders (1872). Illinois R3 status dated "as of October 2026" (the R3 page lists reports through 2025 and a 2026 footer). Presidential pardons reach only federal offenses (constitutional pardon power; general knowledge). Low-risk history piece: no High Society staff stories, events, discounts, donations or sales tie-ins, and no shop or deals links. No Michigan expungement or equity-program law is stated (law-facts has none); the article points to the planned Michigan expungement guide. Cross-check 2026-10-24: wording revised so no span of 8+ words is shared with any other blog article or site page (n-gram check over site/src/content/blog and site/src/content/pages), and the gate’s overlap check passes.
